transcript.content: Hello, welcome. What brings you in to see me today?

I can’t stop fixating on how awful I look on camera and in photos, and it’s starting to affect my work and social life. It has gotten to the point where I'm constantly anxious about how I appear to others, and a close friend finally convinced me that I need to talk to someone about it.
When you look at yourself, is there a specific feature or part of your appearance that you feel is highly flawed or defective, even if others tell you it looks completely fine?

Yes, I'm completely fixated on the dark circles and heavy bags under my eyes, and how bloated and uneven my face looks. Even though my friends and coworkers tell me they don't notice anything wrong, I'm convinced it makes me look incredibly exhausted and sloppy, especially on camera.
Do you find yourself frequently checking your appearance in mirrors, spending a lot of time trying to hide these features, or constantly comparing how you look to others?

Yes, definitely. Before any video call, I spend 30 to 40 minutes adjusting the lighting, testing angles, and redoing my makeup to hide my puffy face and dark circles. During and after events, I constantly stare at my camera box or zoom in on tagged photos, and I keep asking my friends for reassurance about how I looked.
Is your anxiety in social situations mostly driven by worries about people noticing your face and eyes, or do you also worry about things like saying the wrong thing, blushing, or trembling?

My anxiety is almost entirely driven by worries about people noticing my face, specifically my dark circles and bloated appearance. I don't really worry about saying the wrong thing, blushing, or trembling; it's really just about how awful I look.

latest_inference.note: Previously, the candidates were F45.2 (Hypochondriacal disorder / Body Dysmorphic Disorder) and F40.1 (Social Phobia). The patient has clarified that their social anxiety is entirely driven by fear of others noticing their perceived physical flaws (dark circles and bloated face) rather than fear of social performance, trembling, or blushing. This rules out primary Social Phobia (F40.1) and confirms Body Dysmorphic Disorder, which is classified under F45.2 in ICD-10. I am ready to finalize the diagnosis.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a severe preoccupation with perceived defects in their physical appearance (specifically dark circles, under-eye bags, and a bloated, uneven face) that are not noticeable to others. This preoccupation leads to repetitive behaviors such as excessive grooming, adjusting lighting/makeup, checking mirrors/cameras, and seeking reassurance. The symptoms cause significant impairment in social and occupational functioning. Although social anxiety is present, it is exclusively driven by the fear of others noticing these perceived physical flaws rather than a primary fear of social performance, ruling out primary Social Phobia (F40.1). In ICD-10, Body Dysmorphic Disorder is classified under F45.2 (Hypochondriacal disorder).
